title: Historical Development of Chinese Contract Law
content:
# Historical Development of Chinese Contract Law

## Imperial China (pre-1911)
- Whether Imperial China had "civil law" (as opposed to criminal law) is **debatable**: scholars such as **Liang Chichao (梁啟超)** and **Wang Boqi (王伯琦)** argued it did not exist, while **Yang Honglie (楊鴻烈)** held the opposite view.
- What is beyond dispute: **no civil code ever existed** in Imperial China, though there was **separate legislation on marriage and debt**.

## Late Qing: first draft civil code
- **1902**: Emperor Guang Xu formed a team to draft a civil code modelled on **Continental European codes**.
- Drafting ran **1908–1910**, producing the **Draft Civil Law of Great Qing (《大清民律草案》)** — the first civil code in China's history, though only in draft form.
- It was **never enacted**: the Qing Dynasty was overthrown shortly afterwards.

## Republican era: first enacted civil code
- **April 1927**: National Government established; **December 1928**: the Legislative Yuan took charge of drafting.
- **January 1929**: Drafting Committee of the Civil Code set up; compilation began **February 1929**.
- **26 December 1930**: the **Civil Law of the Republic of China (《中華民國民法》)** was promulgated — the first enacted civil code in Chinese history, containing **detailed contract law provisions**.

## People's Republic of China (post-1949)
- **1954**: drafting of a new civil code began; a draft was completed in **December 1956**, but it was never enacted due to the **antirightist movements and the Cultural Revolution**; political unrest ended in **1978**.
- Rather than revive the old draft, China legislated on contract law **piecemeal** to serve the economic reform starting in 1979:
  - **Economic Contract Law (1981)**
  - **Foreign Economic Contract Law (1985)**
  - **Technology Contract Law (1987)**
- The **General Principles of Civil Law (GPCL, 1985)** is **not a civil code** — only "general principles", like the introductory chapter of a still-unfinished code.
- The three contract statutes were **not comprehensive**: they contained **contradictory provisions** with **overlapping scopes**.

## The 1999 unified Contract Law
- **1993**: drafting of a new Contract Law began, intended to replace the three statutes.
- The drafters (largely legal academics) drew extensively on international and comparative sources: the **UNIDROIT Principles of International Commercial Contracts (PICC)**, the **CISG**, the **Principles of European Contract Law (PECL)**, the **French and German civil codes**, and **English common law**.
- **Passed 15 March 1999, effective 1 October 1999**; supplemented by Supreme People's Court judicial interpretations (including on technology and construction contracts).
- The 1999 Contract Law remained unrevised as of the source text's writing.

## Timeline at a glance
| Year | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 1902–1910 | Draft Civil Law of Great Qing (never enacted) |
| 1930 | Civil Law of the Republic of China promulgated |
| 1954–1956 | PRC civil code draft (not enacted) |
| 1981 / 1985 / 1987 | Economic, Foreign Economic, Technology Contract Laws |
| 1985 | General Principles of Civil Law |
| 1993 | Drafting of unified Contract Law begins |
| 1999 | Unified PRC Contract Law (effective 1 Oct 1999) |
